difficultyReason: Two-part antecedent: a physician is justified in withholding information only if (a) disclosure would cause direct psychological harm and (b) the patient has not explicitly requested full disclosure. Traps satisfy only one condition.
stimulus: A physician is justified in withholding a diagnosis from a patient only if two conditions are both met: the disclosure of that diagnosis would foreseeably cause the patient direct psychological harm, and the patient has not explicitly requested complete information about his or her medical condition.
questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Dr. Osei withholds a terminal diagnosis from a patient who has signed a form requesting full disclosure of all medical findings, because Dr. Osei believes the news will cause the patient severe depression.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dr. Reyes withholds a cancer diagnosis from a patient who has never asked about her condition and whose psychiatrist has documented that learning of the diagnosis would trigger a severe anxiety episode.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Dr. Pham discloses a serious diagnosis to a patient who has not asked for information, reasoning that withholding information is generally paternalistic.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Dr. Novak withholds a minor diagnosis from a patient who explicitly asked for complete information, on the grounds that the patient seemed emotionally fragile during the appointment.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Dr. Chen withholds a diagnosis from a patient who has not requested information, even though Dr. Chen believes the disclosure would cause no psychological harm whatsoever.

explanations.correct: Dr. Reyes satisfies both conditions: the patient has never requested full disclosure (condition 2 met) and the psychiatrist's documentation establishes that disclosure would cause direct psychological harm (condition 1 met). The withholding is therefore justified under the principle.
explanations.A: Partial fit / violates the principle: the patient explicitly requested full disclosure, so condition 2 is not met. Withholding is not justified regardless of the anticipated harm.
explanations.C: Outside the principle's scope: the principle governs when withholding is justified; this answer describes disclosure and offers a separate rationale. Neither condition is evaluated.
explanations.D: Partial fit: the patient explicitly asked for complete information, so condition 2 fails. The principle does not justify withholding here.
explanations.E: Partial fit: condition 2 is met (no request for information), but condition 1 fails because disclosure would cause no psychological harm. Withholding is not justified.

difficultyReason: Two-part antecedent: a tenant is entitled to withhold rent only if (a) the landlord has been notified of the defect in writing and (b) the landlord has failed to remedy the defect within a reasonable time. Traps omit one condition.
stimulus: A residential tenant is entitled to withhold rent from a landlord only if the tenant has previously notified the landlord of the defect in writing and the landlord has failed to remedy the defect within a reasonable period of time after receiving that notice.
questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Margolis withholds rent after verbally telling her landlord three times about a broken heating system that has gone unrepaired for four months.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Tremblay withholds rent after sending a written notice about a leaking roof; his landlord repairs the roof within one week of receiving the notice.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Okonkwo sends a written notice about a faulty electrical panel and, after the landlord takes no action for three months, withholds rent.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Svensson withholds rent immediately upon discovering a mold problem, intending to notify the landlord by letter the following day.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Petrakis sends a written notice about a pest infestation and withholds rent the very next day before the landlord has had any opportunity to respond.

explanations.correct: Okonkwo sent written notice (condition 1 met) and the landlord took no action for three months, which constitutes failure to remedy within a reasonable time (condition 2 met). Withholding rent is therefore justified.
explanations.A: Partial fit: the defect went unrepaired for four months (condition 2 met), but Margolis only notified verbally, not in writing (condition 1 not met). Withholding is not justified.
explanations.B: Partial fit / violates the principle: written notice was given (condition 1 met), but the landlord remedied the defect within one week — a reasonable time — so condition 2 is not met.
explanations.D: Violates the principle: Svensson withholds before sending any written notice. Neither condition is met at the time of withholding.
explanations.E: Partial fit: written notice was sent (condition 1 met), but withholding occurred the very next day — not after a reasonable period for the landlord to respond (condition 2 not met).

difficultyReason: Two-part antecedent: a government agency should release a document only if (a) the request is made by an identifiable individual or organization and (b) the document contains no information that would compromise ongoing law-enforcement operations.
stimulus: A government agency should release a requested document to the public only if the request is made by an identifiable individual or recognized organization and the document does not contain information that would compromise an ongoing law-enforcement operation.
questionStem: Which one of the following conforms most closely to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The agency releases a document to an anonymous requester because the document concerns a completed investigation with no bearing on current operations.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The agency releases a document to a registered nonprofit organization, having confirmed that the document references no active investigations.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The agency withholds a document from an identifiable journalist because the agency director personally dislikes the journalist's reporting.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The agency releases a document to an identifiable university research center, even though the document contains details of surveillance methods currently in use.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The agency releases a document to an identifiable law firm, reasoning that law firms are officers of the court and therefore always entitled to government records.

explanations.correct: The request comes from a registered nonprofit organization (identifiable/recognized — condition 1 met), and the document references no active investigations (condition 2 met). Release is justified.
explanations.A: Partial fit: the document condition is met, but the request is anonymous, so condition 1 is not met. Release is not justified.
explanations.C: Outside the principle's scope / violates: the requester is identifiable and the principle is silent on personal animosity; the principle would actually support release if condition 2 were met, but that condition is not addressed here. The withholding is based on an impermissible reason not sanctioned by the principle.
explanations.D: Partial fit / violates the principle: the requester is identifiable (condition 1 met), but the document contains details of currently active surveillance methods, so condition 2 is not met. Release is not justified.
explanations.E: Extra-fact misdirection: the requester is identifiable (condition 1 met), but the answer introduces a separate rationale ('officers of the court') that bypasses the principle's second condition, which is left unsatisfied.

difficultyReason: Two-part antecedent: a corporation is obligated to compensate a worker for an injury only if (a) the injury occurred on company premises during working hours and (b) the worker had complied with all relevant posted safety protocols.
stimulus: A corporation is obligated to compensate an injured worker only if the injury occurred on company premises during scheduled working hours and the worker had complied with all relevant safety protocols posted by the company at the time of the injury.
questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Drummond injures her back while lifting boxes in the company warehouse during her shift, having followed all posted lifting-safety guidelines. The corporation is obligated to compensate her.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ibarra injures his hand on company machinery during his shift, but he had removed a required safety guard moments before the accident. The corporation is obligated to compensate him.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Weston slips on ice in the company parking lot during her lunch break while complying with all posted protocols. The corporation is obligated to compensate her.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Callahan injures his wrist at home while completing a work assignment sent by his supervisor, having followed all company protocols. The corporation is obligated to compensate him.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Nguyen injures her shoulder during an after-hours company social event held on company premises; she had followed all posted protocols. The corporation is obligated to compensate her.

explanations.correct: Drummond's injury occurred on company premises during her scheduled shift (condition 1 met) and she complied with all posted safety protocols (condition 2 met). The corporation is obligated to compensate her.
explanations.B: Partial fit: the injury occurred on premises during working hours (condition 1 met), but Ibarra removed a required safety guard, violating posted protocols (condition 2 not met). No obligation arises.
explanations.C: Partial fit / ambiguous timing: compliance is met (condition 2), but 'lunch break' may not constitute 'scheduled working hours.' Even if it did, this is the intended trap for condition 1.
explanations.D: Partial fit: protocols were followed (condition 2 met), but the injury occurred at home, not on company premises (condition 1 not met). No obligation arises.
explanations.E: Partial fit: the injury occurred on company premises (part of condition 1 met) and protocols were followed (condition 2 met), but an after-hours social event is not 'scheduled working hours' (condition 1 not fully met).

difficultyReason: Two-part antecedent: an art museum is justified in refusing to display a donated work only if (a) the donor's conditions of display conflict with the museum's established curatorial policies and (b) the museum's governing board has formally reviewed and rejected those conditions.
stimulus: An art museum is justified in refusing to display a donated artwork only if the donor's conditions for display conflict with the museum's established curatorial policies and the museum's governing board has formally reviewed and rejected those conditions.
questionStem: Which one of the following conforms most closely to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A museum refuses to display a donated sculpture because the curator personally finds the work aesthetically unappealing, without consulting the governing board.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A museum refuses to display a donated painting because the donor insists it be shown alongside works from a specific period, a condition incompatible with the museum's rotation policy; the board formally voted to reject the condition.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A museum refuses to display a donated photograph because the donor's condition — that it never be loaned to other institutions — conflicts with curatorial policy; the director rejects the condition without board review.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A museum refuses to display a donated tapestry because the donor's lighting requirements are unusual, even though the board approved the donation and the lighting requirement is not addressed in curatorial policy.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A museum refuses to display a donated mosaic after the board reviews the donation file, even though the donor imposed no conditions and the refusal is based solely on lack of gallery space.

explanations.correct: The donor's condition conflicts with the museum's established rotation policy (condition 1 met) and the board formally voted to reject that condition (condition 2 met). The refusal is justified.
explanations.A: Violates the principle: the curator's personal preference is not a conflict with curatorial policy, and the board was not consulted. Neither condition is met.
explanations.C: Partial fit: the conflict with curatorial policy exists (condition 1 met), but the director — not the board — rejected the condition without formal board review (condition 2 not met). Refusal is not justified.
explanations.D: Partial fit / reversed: the board reviewed the donation (condition 2 partially met), but the lighting requirement is not addressed in curatorial policy, so there is no conflict (condition 1 not met). Refusal is not justified.
explanations.E: Outside the principle's scope: the principle governs refusals when donor conditions conflict with policy. Here there are no donor conditions; the refusal is based on lack of space, a scenario the principle does not address.

difficultyReason: Two-part antecedent: a scientist should retract a published finding only if (a) the scientist has discovered a methodological error that materially affects the conclusions and (b) a correction rather than retraction cannot adequately address that error.
stimulus: A scientist should retract a published finding only if the scientist has discovered a methodological error that materially affects the study's conclusions and a published correction would be insufficient to adequately address that error.
questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Dr. Falcone retracts a study after discovering that a mislabeled axis on one figure would mislead readers, even though issuing a corrected figure would fully resolve the problem.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dr. Huang retracts a study after discovering that a transcription error in the data tables fundamentally undermines all of the paper's principal conclusions and cannot be fixed by issuing a correction.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Dr. Mbeki retracts a study after learning that a rival lab has published contradictory findings, even though Dr. Mbeki can find no error in her own methodology.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Dr. Sorensen retracts a study after a peer reviewer raises concerns about the sample size, even though the sample size is consistent with accepted norms in the field and does not affect the conclusions.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Dr. Ivanova retracts a study upon discovering a methodological flaw that affects a secondary analysis but leaves all primary conclusions intact, determining that a correction would be an adequate remedy.

explanations.correct: Dr. Huang discovered a transcription error (a methodological error) that fundamentally undermines all principal conclusions (condition 1: materially affects conclusions — met) and cannot be fixed by a correction (condition 2: correction insufficient — met). Retraction is justified.
explanations.A: Partial fit / violates: there is a methodological error (condition 1 arguably met), but issuing a corrected figure would fully resolve the problem, meaning a correction is sufficient (condition 2 not met). Retraction is not justified.
explanations.C: Outside the principle's scope: contradictory external findings are not a methodological error in the original study. Condition 1 is not met.
explanations.D: Partial fit / violates: the peer reviewer's concern does not constitute a discovered methodological error affecting conclusions (condition 1 not met). Retraction is not justified.
explanations.E: Partial fit: a methodological flaw was found, but it affects only a secondary analysis and the scientist determined a correction is adequate (condition 2 not met). The principle does not justify retraction.

difficultyReason: Two-part antecedent: a school is justified in expelling a student only if (a) the student has committed a violation that is explicitly enumerated in the school's published code of conduct and (b) the student was given a formal warning for a prior violation of the same rule.
stimulus: A school is justified in expelling a student only if the student has committed a violation explicitly enumerated in the school's published code of conduct and the student had previously received a formal written warning for violating the same rule.
questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A school expels Tarrant for cheating on an exam, an offense listed in the code of conduct, after issuing him a formal written warning for cheating earlier in the semester.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A school expels Brennan for repeated tardiness, an offense listed in the code of conduct, after issuing formal written warnings for plagiarism on two prior occasions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A school expels Hollis for using unauthorized software during an exam — conduct not specifically enumerated in the code of conduct — after issuing a written warning for the same conduct.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A school expels Kimura for plagiarism, listed in the code of conduct, without issuing any prior warning because the school principal considers plagiarism a serious offense.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A school expels Oduya for disruptive behavior, listed in the code of conduct, after informally cautioning her about the same behavior at a parent-teacher meeting.

explanations.correct: Cheating is explicitly enumerated in the code of conduct (condition 1 met), and Tarrant had previously received a formal written warning for cheating — the same rule (condition 2 met). Expulsion is justified.
explanations.B: Partial fit: tardiness is listed in the code (condition 1 met), but the prior written warnings were for plagiarism, not tardiness — not the same rule (condition 2 not met). Expulsion is not justified.
explanations.C: Partial fit: a formal written warning was issued for the same conduct (condition 2 met), but using unauthorized software is not enumerated in the code of conduct (condition 1 not met). Expulsion is not justified.
explanations.D: Partial fit: plagiarism is listed in the code (condition 1 met), but no prior formal warning was given (condition 2 not met). The principal's view of seriousness is irrelevant to the principle.
explanations.E: Partial fit: disruptive behavior is listed (condition 1 met), but the prior caution was informal, not a formal written warning (condition 2 not met). Expulsion is not justified.

difficultyReason: Two-part antecedent in a technology domain: a software company is obligated to issue a free patch only if (a) the vulnerability was present in the product at the time of sale and (b) the vulnerability exposes user data to unauthorized external access.
stimulus: A software company is obligated to issue a free security patch to its customers only if the security vulnerability was present in the product at the time it was originally sold and the vulnerability exposes customer data to unauthorized external access.
questionStem: Which one of the following conforms most closely to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Nexara Software issues a free patch after discovering that a feature added in a post-sale update created a flaw allowing outsiders to access user data.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Vortex Technologies issues a free patch after finding that its product, as originally sold, contained a bug that slows processing speeds but does not expose any user data.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Paragon Systems issues a free patch after discovering that its product, as originally sold, contained a flaw that allows unauthorized third parties to extract stored customer records.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lumicon issues a free patch for a vulnerability introduced by a third-party plug-in, not present at sale, which allows outsiders to monitor user keystrokes.

choices.label: E
choices.text: ClarityTech issues a free patch for a vulnerability that was present at the time of sale but that only permits internal employees — not outsiders — to access user data without authorization.

explanations.correct: The flaw was present in the product as originally sold (condition 1 met) and it allows unauthorized third parties to extract customer records, constituting unauthorized external access (condition 2 met). The obligation to issue a free patch is established.
explanations.A: Partial fit: external access to user data exists (condition 2 met), but the flaw was introduced by a post-sale update, not present at time of sale (condition 1 not met). No obligation under the principle.
explanations.B: Partial fit: the vulnerability was present at time of sale (condition 1 met), but it slows processing speeds without exposing user data (condition 2 not met). No obligation under the principle.
explanations.D: Partial fit: external access to user data exists (condition 2 met), but the vulnerability was introduced by a third-party plug-in after the sale (condition 1 not met). No obligation under the principle.
explanations.E: Partial fit: the vulnerability was present at time of sale (condition 1 met), but only internal employees — not unauthorized external parties — can access the data (condition 2 not met). No obligation under the principle.

difficultyReason: Two-part antecedent in a linguistics/history domain: a lexicographer is justified in labeling a word 'archaic' only if (a) the word has not appeared in any widely circulated publication within the past fifty years and (b) the word lacks any living community of speakers who use it in ordinary discourse.
stimulus: A lexicographer is justified in labeling a word 'archaic' only if the word has not appeared in any widely circulated publication within the past fifty years and no living community of speakers uses the word in ordinary discourse.
questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A lexicographer labels 'sooth' archaic after confirming that it has not appeared in any widely circulated publication in over sixty years, even though a small regional dialect community still uses it regularly in conversation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A lexicographer labels 'forsooth' archaic after confirming that it appears only in scholarly articles about Middle English — not in widely circulated publications — and that no living dialect community uses it in everyday speech.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A lexicographer labels 'prithee' archaic because it sounds old-fashioned, without researching whether it appears in current publications or is used by any speaker community.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A lexicographer labels 'perchance' archaic after finding that it appeared in a major newspaper's crossword column last year, reasoning that crossword usage does not constitute serious discourse.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A lexicographer labels 'yclept' archaic after discovering that a popular fantasy novel published fifteen years ago used the term, but no speaker community uses it in ordinary discourse.

explanations.correct: Scholarly articles about Middle English do not constitute widely circulated publications in the relevant sense, so condition 1 is met; and no living dialect community uses 'forsooth' in everyday speech (condition 2 met). The 'archaic' label is justified.
explanations.A: Partial fit: condition 1 is met (not in widely circulated publications for 60+ years), but a small regional dialect community still uses the word in conversation (condition 2 not met). The label is not justified.
explanations.C: Outside the principle's scope / violates: the lexicographer applies no relevant inquiry. Neither condition is verified. The label cannot be justified under the principle.
explanations.D: Partial fit / violates: no living speaker community uses the word (condition 2 met), but the word appeared in a major newspaper last year — a widely circulated publication (condition 1 not met). The label is not justified.
explanations.E: Partial fit: no speaker community uses 'yclept' in ordinary discourse (condition 2 met), but a popular fantasy novel published fifteen years ago — a widely circulated publication — used the term (condition 1 not met). The label is not justified.

difficultyReason: Two-part antecedent in an environmental policy domain: a regulatory agency is justified in imposing an emergency pollution moratorium only if (a) monitoring data show that pollutant levels have exceeded the established safety threshold and (b) the source of the exceedance has been identified as a specific regulated facility.
stimulus: A regulatory agency is justified in imposing an emergency pollution moratorium on a facility only if current monitoring data show that pollutant levels in the affected area have exceeded the established safety threshold and the agency has identified that specific facility as the source of the exceedance.
questionStem: Which one of the following conforms most closely to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The agency imposes a moratorium on the Hartwell plant after monitoring data confirm that pollutant levels in the surrounding watershed exceed the safety threshold and isotopic analysis identifies the Hartwell plant as the source.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The agency imposes a moratorium on the Crestline refinery after receiving citizen complaints about odors, even though current monitoring data show pollutant levels below the safety threshold.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The agency imposes a moratorium on the Delphi chemical plant after monitoring data confirm that safety thresholds are exceeded, even though the agency has not yet determined which facility in the industrial corridor is responsible.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The agency imposes a moratorium on the Solaris factory after identifying it as the source of elevated emissions, even though current data show pollutant levels still within the established safety threshold.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The agency imposes a moratorium on all facilities in a region after a general modeling study predicts that future pollutant levels may exceed the threshold, without having identified any specific source.

explanations.correct: Monitoring data confirm that pollutant levels exceed the safety threshold (condition 1 met), and isotopic analysis identifies the Hartwell plant as the specific source (condition 2 met). The moratorium is justified.
explanations.B: Partial fit / violates: the source is presumably identified (condition 2 arguably met), but monitoring data show levels below the threshold (condition 1 not met). The moratorium is not justified.
explanations.C: Partial fit: monitoring data confirm threshold exceedance (condition 1 met), but the agency has not identified which specific facility is responsible (condition 2 not met). The moratorium is not justified.
explanations.D: Partial fit: the facility has been identified as a source (condition 2 met), but current pollutant levels remain within the safety threshold (condition 1 not met). The moratorium is not justified.
explanations.E: Violates both conditions: modeling predictions are not current monitoring data exceeding the threshold (condition 1 not met), and no specific facility has been identified (condition 2 not met). The moratorium is not justified.
